name: Brennan Center for Justice (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults: the tariff ruling's gain abroad (about 48%, China's, net of small losses elsewhere) and the rest in the United States (the tariff ruling at home, democracy, prisons and jails).
summary: The Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan law and policy institute in New York and Washington, spent $57.6 million in the year to June 2025 on research, litigation and advocacy for voting rights and fair elections, checks on presidential power, and ending mass incarceration. Three branches: its 1.2% share of the litigation that ended the emergency tariffs in February 2026 (about 0.12% of long-run US GDP restored, and more than as much again for trading partners, China above all), half of it done in the year; its 2% share of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (the shared 11%, cut by about a twentieth), valued by the income a slide would cost as it builds up; and its 1.6% share of the reform field's part in the fall in incarceration, valued by prisoners' wellbeing and shortened lives. With its next dollar at 32% of the average (it holds about two years of spending in liquid reserves), it comes to about 0.07 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, four fifths of it from the tariff ruling. The result is mostly uncertainty (the Center's share of the tariff litigation, the years a win counts, the field's effect on the breakdown risk; the model's own ranges alone span several hundredfold), and all three branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Brennan Center's own spending in the year to 30 June 2025 on its six programme columns, with its share of management and fundraising, split between the democracy work (Democracy, Liberty and National Security: the breakdown-risk and tariff branches) and the justice branch by their direct spending. From the audited statement of functional expenses; donated legal services are left out.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Who the work reaches: everyone governed by US democracy and paying US tariffs (democracy and tariff branches) and the people kept out of prison each year by the national decline in incarceration (justice branch).

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the work changes: the chance that US democracy breaks down, valued by the income a breakdown would cost; the income the emergency tariffs cost the US and its trading partners until the courts struck them down; and years out of prison, valued by wellbeing and the deaths that prison causes. Each counts the whole field's or the whole litigation's effect; the Center's share is in the adjustments.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the estimate, the Brennan Center's share of its field's resources, and missing data; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Chance the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (about 11%, 5% to 28%): the stake the democracy work acts on. A cut in a chance is counted at its expected value, as the catastrophic-risk models count a cut in a hazard: the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet, so it isn't a single event.

rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a slide
rows.explainer: Breakdown risk × the field's relative cut; the Brennan Center's share of the field is in dem_attribution_share.

rows.label: Years from the work until a slide it averts would have come
rows.explainer: The forecast counts the Economist's reports published before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so the window left covers 2026 to 2028, and a slide averted would on average have come in its middle, 2027: about two and a half years after the year to June 2025 (1.5 to 4.5), as in the Protect Democracy model's three years after its calendar 2024.

rows.label: Rate for the slide's loss: the shared discount rate plus the reversal hazard
rows.explainer: The loss averted lasts only while the slide would have lasted.

rows.label: Years over which a slide's income loss builds up
rows.explainer: The shared figure (about 25 years, 20 to 30).

rows.label: Discounted years of the full loss averted by putting a slide off
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + dem_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + dem_rate) ^ (0 - dem_ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + dem_rate) * ln(1 + dem_rate) * dem_ramp_years) * dem_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp: a slide's loss builds evenly over dem_ramp_years; putting the slide off by the years counted ($win_years_counted) moves the whole ramp later, so the loss avoided rises to a fifth of the full loss over the first five years, stays there until the ramp is complete and falls back to nothing five years later, years_of_impact full-loss years in all before discounting. Its present value (continuous form) at dem_rate, times the wait at the shared rate: about 1.5 full-loss years at the defaults.

source.title: The Budget Lab at Yale, State of U.S. Tariffs: March 9, 2026
source.page: pp. 5-6, table 1, row 'Percent change in long-run GDP' (columns: before the ruling; immediately after it, no IEEPA or Section 122; 10% Section 122 expiring; extended; 15% Section 122 expiring; extended)

rows.explainer: All 2025 tariffs left US GDP 0.25% smaller in the long run before the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling that the IEEPA tariffs exceeded the president's authority; after it, 0.07% if the 10% Section 122 replacement expires after 150 days (0.18% restored, the high end), 0.13% if it is made permanent (0.12% restored, the best guess: Section 122 expired on 24 July 2026 and was replaced by Section 301 duties of about 10-12.5% on most imports, close to that scenario) and 0.18% for a permanent 15% rate (0.07%, the low end). GDP, not tariff revenue: the duties and refunds are transfers.

rows.label: Trading partners' gains from the ruling, as a multiple of the US gain

source.title: The Budget Lab at Yale, State of U.S. Tariffs: January 19, 2026 (before the ruling) and March 9, 2026 (after it)
source.page: fig. 4 in both reports (long-run change in real GDP level by region); the March report is https://budgetlab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/page_to_pdf/1410/publication_1410.pdf
source.note: Long-run real GDP, percentage points, January (current policy, before the ruling) to March (Section 122 extended): China -0.23 to -0.16, Canada -0.22 to -0.21, Mexico +0.02 to -0.04, other free-trade partners +0.05 to +0.03, EU +0.04 to +0.03, UK +0.10 to +0.05, Japan and the rest about unchanged.

rows.explainer: The tariffs were levied on partners' goods and shrink their economies too, so the ruling's direct effect reaches them: part of the main chain, not a spillover. Valued as the US gain is (population × ln(1 + change in GDP)), China's 1.4 billion people gaining 0.07 points of GDP outweigh the small losses of Mexico, the EU and the UK (whose exporters lose the edge the IEEPA tariffs gave them over China): about 0.8 million ln-units a year abroad against 0.41 million in the US at the best guess (×2.0), or ×1.3 against the US change in the same two reports (-0.31 to -0.13). 1.6 times the US gain, from 1.3 to 2: between the like-for-like ratio (both changes from the same two reports, 1.3) and the ratio to the model's own US gain (2.0), since the US change in those two reports (0.18 points) includes the Section 122 scenario's own assumptions while the model's best guess (0.12 points) is the extended-replacement case.

rows.label: Income gained from the ruling in the US and abroad, units of value (before adjustments)
rows.formula: us_population * tar_ln_gain * (1 + tar_abroad_multiple) * $uov_per_ln_consumption * tar_p_success * tar_discounted_years * tar_cost_year_share

rows.label: Amici's share of all the resources behind the litigation
rows.explainer: Anchored on countable effort. At the Supreme Court the amici wrote more than the parties: about 37 briefs of up to 8,000 words each (Supreme Court Rule 33.1(g), against 13,000 for a party's merits brief) beside the parties' six merits briefs and replies, up to about four times the parties' words (a ceiling: briefs often run shorter than the limit). But the parties' counsel (the Liberty Justice Center for the importers in V.O.S. Selections, Akin Gump for Learning Resources, twelve states' attorneys general) also built the record, briefed and argued every motion and appeal at four levels of court and argued the cases, which amici never do, and most of an amicus brief's value is in the few the justices draw on. 15%, from 5% (the parties' work as most of the effort) to 35% (counting words alone, discounted for the arguments and the record).

rows.label: People per year newly kept out of prison or jail by the US decline in incarceration

source.title: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Correctional Populations in the United States, 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310413, September 2025), table 1

rows.explainer: The yearly flow of the decline (Convention 3): 2,222,500 people incarcerated in 2013 and 2,086,000 in 2019 (the same column: '2019 6,343,200 4,357,500 3,492,900 878,700 2,086,000'), 136,500 fewer over six years, 22,750 a year, the years before the pandemic that the field's spending below also comes from. High: 2013-2023 (369,600 fewer, 36,960 a year), inflated by the pandemic's releases. Low: since 2021 the incarcerated population has risen (1,776,000 in 2021, 1,852,900 in 2023), so the field's yearly gain may now be near nothing.

rows.label: Share of the decline caused by policy changes (sentencing, bail, parole, drug laws)
rows.explainer: Over 2013-2019 violent crime was about flat while property crime and arrests fell (FBI Uniform Crime Reports), routes to fewer prisoners that aren't reform; states passed justice-reinvestment, sentencing and bail laws and Congress the First Step Act (2018). 60%, from 30% to 85%, allows for the fall in property crime and arrests: no study apportions the national decline.

rows.label: Share of those policy changes owed to the reform advocacy field
rows.explainer: Against officials, budgets, courts and prosecutors elected on reform: the advocacy field (research, campaigns, coalitions across left and right) is credited with 40%, from 15% to 70%, a judgment like IRAP's advocacy model's share of the refugee programme's rebuild owed to advocacy.
